definition: Stoic means enduring hardship without showing feeling or complaint.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word stoic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know stoic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Grandmother was stoic about the eviction, packing sixty years of life into boxes without a word of complaint.
Composed only means self-possessed — your voice steady even as your eyes shine; stoic asks more.
Uncomplaining bears the hardship without protest, though a wince may escape; stoic goes further and lets nothing escape at all.
Unfeeling outruns stoic and changes the claim: the stoic patient feels every ache and shows none, while an unfeeling one has nothing to hide — stoicism ends where feeling does.

Impassive means showing no emotion at all — a blank, unreadable face — with no claim about what is being endured; a poker player is impassive over a winning hand. Stoic requires hardship: feeling mastered while something genuinely hard is borne. Every stoic face is impassive, but only suffering makes it stoic.

Unflinching means not recoiling at the moment of impact — the bad news lands, the needle goes in, and you do not pull away. It describes one instant of steadiness under something sharp. Stoic covers the long haul: hardship endured for weeks or years with no complaint and no display.

Stoic comes from one particular building — the Stoa Poikile, the painted porch where Zeno lectured around 300 BC. Greek stoa never spread into other English words, so the porch survives only here, hidden inside a word about keeping feeling off your face.
Stoic means enduring hardship without showing feeling or complaint.
The soldier's letters home were famously stoic: three lines about the weather, a question about the dog, nothing at all of the shelling that his unit's diary recorded almost nightly.
Only after the war, reading that diary, did his family learn what the calm pages had been written through.
Stoic is exactly right because the feeling exists and is mastered: he suffered the shelling and let none of it reach the page.
Numb would mean the feeling was gone; composed would say only that he kept control, without the hardship that stoic requires.
Stoic is usually a compliment: hardship met with silence and steadiness.

Keep it apart from its cluster-mates — apathetic means the caring is missing, while the stoic cares intensely and shows nothing; sobriety is the grave manner an audience sees, while stoic is endurance the audience may never learn about.
If there is no hardship, the word does not apply.

In 1912, the men of one Antarctic sledging party spent five weeks hauling their gear across sea ice after their ship was crushed, rationing biscuits and sleeping in bags frozen stiff.
The expedition diaries are strangely quiet about pain.
Frostbitten fingers appear in the medical notes, never in complaints.
One geologist, whose feet had blistered so badly he could not remove his boots, was described by his tentmates as stoic: he hauled his full share every day and mentioned the boots only when asked.
This was partly culture and partly survival.
Complaint, the leader wrote, spends strength the ice will bill you for.
Read today, the diaries feel less like heroics than like a long, deliberate refusal to let suffering set the tone.
